lines: Watch the gap between these two boxes. Day one, this choice looks purely operational — less to manage, someone else runs the storage.
Later is where the real cost shows up, and notice it was never about performance. It was always about whose bucket this was.
Before I answer, think about what actually makes data hard to move. It isn't the vendor's name on the bill.
Of these four setups, which one leaves you with bytes that nothing else can read, sitting somewhere you never controlled?
answer: The vendor's own storage, holding the vendor's own format — that combination is the trap.
Notice it's not either one alone. A vendor's bucket with an open format inside it is still fine. It's both together that costs you.

lines: Four platforms, four honest answers to the same question. Watch which word changes each time: yours, theirs, theirs again, yours.
That single word is doing more work than anything else in this whole comparison.
Don't let the word open do the work here — look at what's actually written to disk by default.
One copy of the same files, read two different ways, is a genuinely open format. A table that only opens up once you ask it to is something else.
Resist grouping these four into one feature. A pointer that moves nothing and a copy that moves everything are not the same mechanism wearing two names.
Ask, for each one: did any byte actually move, or did only the ability to see it move?
Same job, run four times, priced four honestly different ways. Watch which lever would actually lower each bar — they're not the same lever.
Shrinking a job's run time helps directly here, does almost nothing there, because the meter underneath isn't counting the same thing.
Here's the part worth sitting with: nothing changed about the data itself between these two bars. Only where it already lived, and in what shape.
One of these numbers is zero because the hard part was already done, months before anyone asked to leave.
If you only remember one line: the owner of the storage is the fact everything else in this comparison quietly depends on.
Open format is a property of the bytes, zero-copy is four different mechanisms, and the meter you're billed under decides which lever actually helps.
Before I answer, notice what this team actually cares about: not today's bill, not how easily they can share data. Specifically, the day they leave.
Out of everything covered, which single fact decides that day?
answer: Storage ownership and open format, together — not the pricing model, not the sharing mechanism.
Those other two matter while you stay. Only ownership and format decide what happens the day you actually go.
